passages.t: Foxes, fire, and a cycle of revenge
passages.happening:
At the time of the wheat harvest Samson takes a young goat as a gift and goes to visit his wife, but her father will not let him in. He had thought Samson hated her, he says, so he gave her to one of Samson's companions. He offers him her younger sister instead (verses 1-2).

Samson answers, “This time I will be blameless in doing harm to the Philistines” (verse 3). He catches three hundred foxes, ties them in pairs by their tails with a torch between each pair, sets the torches alight and lets them loose in the Philistines' standing grain. The grain, the vineyards and the olive groves burn (verses 4-5).

The Philistines ask who did it, and they are told it was Samson, because his wife had been given to his companion. “So the Philistines went up and burned her and her father to death” (verse 6).

Samson tells them, “Because you have done this, I will not rest until I have taken vengeance upon you” (verse 7). He strikes them with a great slaughter and goes to live in a cave in the rock of Etam (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 14 ended with Samson's bride given to his companion and Samson going home angry. This chapter follows what came next, and it is a spiral of revenge. Each side pays the other back, and each payment is worse.

Some readers think this was a marriage in which the wife stayed in her father's house and the husband visited her, a form known in the ancient world. That would explain why Samson comes to her father's house with a gift.

The wheat harvest came in late spring and early summer. Burning ripe grain at that season destroyed a year's food, and the vineyards and olive groves were the region's other great crops. For farming people it was a terrible blow. The Hebrew word for the animals can mean foxes or jackals. Jackals run in packs and would have been easier to catch in such numbers. Readers differ.

Then the worst act in the chapter. The Philistines burn Samson's wife and her father to death. It is exactly what the men of Timnah had threatened her with in chapter 14 if she did not get the riddle's answer. She did what they asked, and they killed her anyway. She never speaks in the story, and she pays for the quarrel of the men around her.

In that world, an insult or an injury to a family demanded an answer, and the answer invited another. Samson's own words show the logic: he is paying back what was done to him. The law of Moses had tried to limit revenge by putting justice in the hands of judges and keeping punishment in proportion. This chapter shows vengeance with no limit at all.
passages.later:
The law's rule of an eye for an eye was given to set a limit: “eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Exodus 21:24), no more than the harm done.

Scripture forbids the endless payback the chapter shows: “Do not say, ‘I will avenge this evil!’ Wait on the LORD, and He will save you” (Proverbs 20:22). Paul wrote, “Do not repay anyone evil for evil” (Romans 12:17).
passages.asks: In this chapter every wrong is paid back with a worse one, and the people who suffer most never chose the fight. Ask where a cycle of payback is running in your family, your work or your town, and who is getting hurt who never chose it. Then ask what it would take for you to be the one who stops paying back.

passages.t: Bound by Judah, and the jawbone
passages.happening:
The Philistines come up and camp in Judah, near a place called Lehi. When the men of Judah ask why, they say they have come to arrest Samson and pay him back (verses 9-10).

Three thousand men of Judah go to Samson's cave. “Do you not realize that the Philistines rule over us? What have you done to us?” Samson answers, “I have done to them what they did to me” (verse 11). They tell him they have come to tie him up and hand him over. He makes them swear not to kill him themselves, and they bind him with two new ropes and lead him away (verses 12-13).

At Lehi the Philistines come out shouting against him. “And the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him. The ropes on his arms became like burnt flax, and the bonds broke loose from his hands” (verse 14). He finds the fresh jawbone of a donkey and strikes down a thousand men with it (verse 15).

He sings: “With the jawbone of a donkey I have piled them into heaps. With the jawbone of a donkey I have slain a thousand men” (verse 16). He throws the jawbone away and names the place Ramath-lehi (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Judah, the largest tribe in the south, had been the first to go up and fight in chapter 1. Now it has accepted Philistine rule. Its men say so plainly: ‘the Philistines rule over us’. Rather than rally to the man God had raised up, three thousand of them come to hand him over, to keep the peace with their masters.

Samson's answer, ‘I have done to them what they did to me’, sums up the whole chapter.

Lehi means jawbone. Its exact place is not known, nor is the rock of Etam's, though an Etam near Bethlehem is named elsewhere.

A fresh jawbone would be heavy and strong, not dry and brittle like an old one, which is why the text says it was fresh. It was also a piece of a dead animal, and Samson's story keeps bringing him into contact with death.

His song is a play on words. In Hebrew the word for donkey and the word for heap sound the same. It is a boast, and it is all about himself. He does not mention God.
passages.later: Judah's surrender stands in sharp contrast to its beginning in this book: “The LORD was with Judah, and they took possession of the hill country” (Judges 1:19). Long afterwards, another son of Judah would be anointed in Bethlehem and would fight the Philistines in God's name: “the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward” (1 Samuel 16:13).
passages.asks: The men of Judah handed over their own deliverer to keep the peace with the people who ruled them. Ask when keeping the peace has been, for you, a failure of courage or of loyalty. And look at Samson's song. Ask whether you tell the story of your victories with God in it, or only yourself.

passages.t: Thirst, and the spring of the one who called
passages.happening:
Samson is very thirsty, and he cries out to the LORD. “You have accomplished this great deliverance through Your servant. Must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?” (verse 18).

“So God opened up the hollow place in Lehi, and water came out of it. When Samson drank, his strength returned, and he was revived” (verse 19). He names the spring En-hakkore, and it is still there in Lehi ‘to this day’.

“And Samson judged Israel for twenty years in the days of the Philistines” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
This is the first time Samson is recorded praying. It comes when he is at the end of his strength, afraid of dying of thirst. And it is the first time he gives the credit to God: ‘You have accomplished this great deliverance through Your servant’. The word for deliverance means rescue or victory, and it ties his personal fight to Israel's need to be rescued.

God answers a man whose life has been run by his own desires. He opens the ground and gives water.

The place names keep both sides of the story. Ramath-lehi, the hill of the jawbone, remembers his strength. En-hakkore means the spring of the one who called. It remembers his need.

The closing note, that he judged Israel twenty years in the days of the Philistines, sounds like the end of a story. But the next chapter will tell how it really ended.
passages.later:
God gave water from the rock to Israel in the desert too: “And when you strike the rock, water will come out of it for the people to drink” (Exodus 17:6).

A psalm says what Samson found at En-hakkore: “In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried to my God for help. From His temple He heard my voice” (Psalm 18:6).
passages.hard:
Does God approve of Samson's violence, since the Spirit rushes on him and God answers his prayer?

The chapter tells the violence without making it a model. Samson's motive is plainly revenge, and he says so. The Philistines' burning of his wife is brutal, and his slaughter in return is out of all proportion. The narrator neither praises nor condemns directly, as often in Judges, and lets the reader see what follows.

At the same time the Spirit of the LORD rushes on Samson (verse 14), and God answers his prayer (verse 19). Readers hold these together in different ways. Some stress that God was using Samson's actions to begin Israel's rescue from the Philistines, as 13:5 and 14:4 said, and that the Spirit's power shows God's purpose in spite of Samson's motives. Others stress that the narrator's silence invites moral judgment, and that Samson's story shows what happens when a leader's gift is not matched by his character.

Both readings recognize that the Bible describes much that it does not approve. God's answering a man does not make the man's every act right.
passages.asks: Samson called on God only when he was about to die of thirst. Ask what it takes for you to admit that you depend on God. And remember that God answered him anyway. Ask what spring God might open for you if you stopped boasting and called.
